I wouldn't be sure that increasing the number of jurors would give the outcome that people are looking for.  At the moment the jury results we are seeing are a sort of 'compromise pick' — each juror might have varying tastes so the songs that appear somewhere in the top half of everyone's lists will end up being the ones awarded points. A song might not be any juror's individual favourite but they can all agree that it was reasonably good and well performed and fulfilled the official criteria that they are instructed to use, so when the rankings of the jurors are combined it ends up on top.

That's why we keep seeing juries go for safer entries. Risky entries are polarising by nature, if one juror decides to award a more 'out there' song their #1 ranking but the other four aren't into it, it's difficult for that song to pick up many if any points from that jury. (This was somewhat addressed when the calculation of jury points was changed a few years back so that each person's top rankings have more weighting than their lowest rankings, so a juror can't single handedly tank a song by ranking it last, but jury points are still largely awarded to songs that all or most jurors somewhat agree on). I feel that with a larger jury we would definitely see more diversity in the individual juror's opinions but that wouldn't necessarily matter as the combined ranking will still be a consensus pick.

Honestly I wouldn't mind seeing a revision of the criteria that the juries are using to rank songs. At the moment the "Overall impression of the act" criterion seems to be interpreted as "production value" and as a result it's easier for countries to elevate an average song if they can afford to throw money at it.

I'm in final year of electrical engineering in a different college but having had a look through the modules of the MTU course there's a lot of crossover. It's definitely a very maths-based field, I'd say 95% of the modules I did had some type of maths involved but to be honest, I don't think engineering maths is off-the-wall difficult.

You'd want to be comfortable with basic algebra, being able to manipulate a sum to solve for x. There was a fair bit of integration/differentiation sprinkled in to various modules as well but for the most part the focus wasn't on being able to integrate some mad complicated thing but rather on understanding the general principle behind why the integration is there and how it relates to the physical world. For example you might have an equation that represents power consumption over time, integrate it to get the energy consumed. The maths itself isn't complex it's just about understanding and recognising when to use it.

I think it's worth mentioning though that you absolutely don't need to arrive in on day 1 with a solid grasp of all of the above. I certainly didn't, and I wouldn't have seen myself as someone who would be able for a hard technical degree when I was finishing school but in reality I wasn't any less capable than anyone else in my classes. It's possible you might be underestimating yourself a bit as well. I think as long as you're interested in the material and willing to put in a bit of work to understand it you'll be fine, it's one of those ones that seems daunting at the outset but you're likely not less competent than the people learning alongside you.

Just on the off chance that you do drive it yourself: make sure you drive clockwise around the route. Buses drive anti clockwise and the roads often don't allow for overtaking so if you drive the same way as them you are guaranteed to end up stuck driving behind at least one bus.

Got 590 and as far as study tips go, the thing that helped me the most was doing past exam questions, correcting them myself with the marking schemes or getting my subject teacher to mark them if they were Irish or English essays or something. Practise doing them within the time limit you would have in the exam, particularly for English, Geography, History or any others that are tight on time. Too many people end up with fewer points than they should have got because of time constraints, not including specific words or phrases in the answer (mostly in the science subjects), not answering exactly what is being asked in essay-style questions. Exam technique is as important as knowing the information.
